extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners involved in peer review workflows (conference chairs, journal editors, grant managers) and developers of automated reviewer-assignment systems
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic review of methods, data sources, and constraints for assigning expert reviewers to proposals (conference/journal papers and grant applications), including representation, similarity computation, COI detection, and optimization. Intended to classify approaches and identify gaps and future directions in RAP research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven important points for fair reviewer assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: When assigning reviewers the following should be considered: (1) reviewers must be assigned to proposals based on their areas of expertise; (2) proposals must be evaluated by the most qualified reviewers in their respective subject areas; (3) reviewers should be eager and enthusiastic about examining proposals; (4) no reviewer should examine more than the agreed-upon number of proposals; (5) each reviewer should analyze the same number of proposals; (6) each proposal should be reviewed by a certain number of reviewers; and (7) relationships between applicants and reviewers that may undermine the fairness of the review process should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These seven points are presented as the key desiderata that motivate automated RAP solutions; they imply requirements on profiling, preference elicitation (willingness/bidding), capacity constraints, coverage (number of reviews per proposal), load balancing, and conflict-of-interest avoidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-based RAP process (representation, similarity, optimization)
rubrics_metrics.description: The RAP process is divided into three stages: (1) creating reviewer and proposal profiles using different information sources to represent candidate reviewers and proposals, (2) calculating a similarity score for every possible proposal-reviewer pair based on the profiles, and (3) optimizing the assignment to maximize similarity score under constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this three-stage decomposition as an organizing framework: ensure robust profile construction (stage 1), sound relevance/similarity modeling (stage 2), and constrained optimization considering practical limits (stage 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of reviewers: use of published-paper metadata and personal attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer profiles commonly use information from reviewers’ published papers (title, abstract, keywords, full text, reference list, citation list, metadata) and personal information (name, affiliation, title, interest area, expertise area, h-index, citation network, co-author information, relationships, reputation/seniority, past evaluation experience, proposal application experience, project management experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine multiple information sources (e.g., abstract+title, or full text where available) to more accurately represent expertise; be aware that self-declared expertise may be subjective and incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of reviewers: self-declared info and preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer representation may include self-declared keywords and reviewer preferences about proposals (self-evaluations for each proposal, degree of willingness per proposal, expressed interest topics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manual information-based approaches require collecting this explicit input (bids, topics, ratings) and can improve matching when available, but require reviewer effort and can be incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of proposals: textual and metadata sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal profiles can be constructed from title, keywords, abstract, full text, subject, research/expertise area, references, citation information, co-author information, applicant's institution, and discipline/specialty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full text usage has grown (especially post-2014) due to improved text/word representation techniques; abstracts and keywords remain commonly used when full text is unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity score as expertise-match indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute a similarity score for every proposal-reviewer pair that captures the expertise match between reviewer and proposal; a higher similarity score indicates a higher expected review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarity computation is the primary output of IRRAP methods and should be well-calibrated to downstream optimization objectives; different similarity models have different strengths (semantic vs word-level vs network-based).

rubrics_metrics.name: IRRAP category: manual information-based approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign reviewers using additional information explicitly provided by reviewers, e.g., reviewers' stated interests, ratings about proposals, topics they provide about themselves, and bidding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These approaches typically require soliciting explicit inputs from reviewers; they can be precise but rely on reviewer participation and truthful reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRRAP category: text-based/content-based approaches (semantic and word-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use NLP/statistical text techniques to model word co-occurrence and semantics in documents: topic models (word-topic-document relations), language models, and word-embedding models. Text-based approaches split into semantic-based and word-based methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose methods according to available text (title/abstract/full text) and desired granularity; semantic/topic models capture themes, embeddings capture fine-grained lexical similarity; recent pre-trained language models improve representation quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRRAP category: network-based approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit network relationships such as citation networks, co-authorship networks, collaboration networks, and other reviewer–reviewer or reviewer–proposal relations to aid matching and COI detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Network-based signals can detect expertise via social/academic structure and help infer latent relationships that text alone misses; combine with textual signals for robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: ORAP category: optimization-based approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform similarity scores and constraints into an optimization problem (operations research) that finds assignments maximizing objectives (e.g., total similarity) subject to constraints (workload, conflicts, coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model choices (integer programming, greedy heuristics, OWA, etc.) and algorithmic solutions should reflect practical scale and required constraints; some systems combine IRRAP similarity scores with ORAP optimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimization objective: maximize aggregate similarity under constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual optimization goal is to maximize the similarity score (or aggregated match quality) between proposals and assigned reviewers while respecting constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about objective aggregation (sum, min, order-weighted averages) and whether fairness or worst-case guarantees are desired in addition to aggregate quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraint: reviewer workload limits (capacity)
rubrics_metrics.description: No reviewer should examine more than an agreed-upon number of proposals; reviewers have maximum capacities that must not be exceeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model reviewer capacity as hard constraints in optimization; consider realistic variability (availability windows, differing capacities) and enforce to avoid reviewer overload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraint: balanced workload across reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Desideratum that each reviewer should analyze the same number of proposals (or that workload be balanced across reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Load balancing can be encoded as constraints or as part of the objective (fairness term); different fairness formulations (equal counts vs bounded deviation) produce different trade-offs with similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraint: coverage — number of reviewers per proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Each proposal should be reviewed by a certain (required) number of reviewers; assignment must meet per-proposal demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat per-proposal required reviewer counts as hard constraints; this interacts with reviewer capacity and may require trade-offs when reviewer pool is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraint: conflict of interest avoidance (COI detection & exclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect and avoid relationships between applicants and reviewers that may undermine fairness, including definite COIs (co-authorship, colleague, advisee-advisor, project collaborators, competitor relationships) and latent COIs (friends, close collaborators, family, etc.) that must be inferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use self-declaration for definite COIs but augment with automatic detection via co-authorship graphs, academic/professional networks, affiliation overlap, and path-distance or weighted relationship models to find latent COIs; treat detected COIs as hard prohibitions or penalized constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: COI handling: self-declaration limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-declaration procedures (asking reviewers/applicants to disclose COIs) are common but time-consuming and potentially incomplete because authors/reviewers may unintentionally or intentionally miss COIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement self-declaration with automated methods; provide tools to ease declaration (pre-filled lists, recommended latent COIs) and iterative updating with historical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: COI detection: use of heterogeneous public sources and weighted relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatic COI detection can retrieve heterogeneous associations from public sources (DBLP, affiliation histories) to construct a heterogeneous publication/academic network; weighted relations (co-authorship strength, co-working duration) can signal latent COIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct knowledge-bases from multiple sources and apply supervised ranking or factor-graph models to recommend latent COIs and iteratively improve detection with historical declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of datasets and privacy considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Real reviewer and proposal assignment data are often not publicly available due to privacy concerns; researchers rely on created datasets and benchmarks where available (listed in appendices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building or evaluating RAP systems, account for data privacy, anonymization, and possible biases introduced by public/synthetic datasets; benchmark on multiple datasets where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reviewer reputation/seniority and past evaluation experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer attributes such as reputation, seniority, h-index, past evaluation experience, project application experience, and project quality can be used to assess reviewer suitability beyond topical expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate reputation metrics when desirable (e.g., for calibrating reviewer reliability), but be cautious about introducing biases or disadvantaging early-career reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate reviewer preferences/willingness (bids) into assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer bidding (willingness to review particular papers) and explicit preferences can and should be used to inform assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model preferences as hard constraints when required (e.g., unwilling = cannot assign) or as soft preferences in the objective; collect bids efficiently to reduce workload on reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple signals for robust matching
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective RAP approaches often combine text-based similarity, network signals, manual declarations, and reviewer/ proposal metadata to create richer profiles and more accurate similarity scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design ensemble or hybrid methods that weight and fuse complementary signals, and validate combinations on diverse datasets and application areas (conference, journal, grant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Different application-area distinctions (conference vs journal vs project proposals)
rubrics_metrics.description: RAP differs by application area: conference assignments are typically global and simultaneous with fixed deadlines; journal assignments are sequential and handled individually; project-proposal assignments may involve different dataset usages and constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor profiling, similarity computation, and optimization strategies to the application (e.g., global optimization for conferences, sequential recommendation for journals) and dataset availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify RAP solutions as IRRAP vs ORAP
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaches for stages 2 and 3 are divided into two main categories: Information Retrieval-based RAP (IRRAP) focusing on similarity computation, and Optimization-based RAP (ORAP) focusing on mathematical models and algorithms for assignment under constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When developing or evaluating solutions, be explicit about which category a method belongs to and whether it addresses one or multiple stages of the RAP pipeline.
